ledger.sentence: A gastroscopy is a test in which a thin, flexible tube with a small camera goes into the mouth, or sometimes the nose, and down into the stomach.
The doctor or nurse watches the lining of the gullet, stomach and the first part of the small bowel on a screen.
ledger.note: Textbook description of upper GI; NHS page title only retrieved.

ledger.sentence: Tiny tissue samples, called biopsies, may be taken, and this is painless.
The stomach must be empty, so trusts ask people to stop eating for about six hours beforehand.
Clear fluids are usually allowed in small sips until about two hours before the test.
One trust explains that an empty stomach matters because sedation can allow food to enter the lungs and cause an infection.
People usually choose between a throat spray and sedation.
The throat spray is a local anaesthetic that numbs the back of the throat, and the person stays awake while a nurse talks them through the test.
For sedation, a small tube called a cannula is placed in a vein, usually in the back of the hand.
The medicine makes the person relaxed and drowsy, but not fully asleep, and they may not remember the test afterwards.
Air is passed in to inflate the stomach, which can cause bloating and burping.
The test usually takes between 5 and 20 minutes.
Common effects include a sore throat and stomach discomfort, which pass within a few hours.
After a throat spray, people can usually leave straight away, though the throat stays numb for up to an hour and eating and drinking wait until the feeling returns.
After sedation, the person rests in a recovery area for a couple of hours.
They need to bring someone with them and go home by car or taxi, because the sedative can stay in the body for 24 hours.
Leaflets advise avoiding driving, alcohol and signing important documents for 24 hours.
Serious complications are rare, and one leaflet says they occur in fewer than 1 in 500 tests.
Possible problems include a tear in the gut wall that may need surgery, bleeding, and an allergic reaction to the sedation or throat spray.
Sedation can affect breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, which is why staff monitor them.
Rare complications include damage to loose teeth, crowns or bridgework.
A leaflet says to call 999 or go to A&E if stomach pain gets worse or if the person vomits blood.
People are told the main findings before they leave and get a written summary to take home.
Biopsy results from the laboratory are not available on the day.
They go to the GP or specialist and usually take two to three weeks.
A gastroscopy passes a thin, flexible tube with a camera through the mouth and down to the stomach.
The stomach needs to be empty, and trusts ask for a fast of several hours beforehand.
People can have a throat spray and stay awake, or sedation that leaves them relaxed and drowsy.
Serious complications are rare, but a person who has severe stomach pain or vomits blood afterwards should call 999 or go to A&E.
ledger.note: Summary: Call 999 or go to A&E if stomach pain gets worse or vomit blood.

ledger.sentence: A gastroscopy uses a thin camera to look at the gullet and stomach. This guide covers fasting, throat spray or sedation, risks and results.
